title: Embodied Grief in the Shadow of Violence: An Integrative Conceptual Review of Widowhood, Trauma, and Social Constraint
abstract: Violent widowhood remains among the least theorized forms of bereavement. While dominant Western psychological models have advanced grief theory, they do not adequately explain grief following intentional spousal loss amid violence, ongoing threat, and gendered social regulation. This integrative conceptual review synthesizes interdisciplinary and cross-cultural scholarship on violent widowhood, traumatic bereavement, embodiment, structural violence, and social constraint to develop a context-sensitive framework for grief after intentional spousal loss. Four interrelated dimensions are identified: traumatic bereavement, embodied grief, gendered and culturally situated mourning, and structural violence under enduring threat. These conditions are argued to fundamentally shape grief in violent widowhood. Rather than following a linear recovery trajectory, grief is conceptualized as an ongoing process of negotiating identity, embodiment, and social belonging. The proposed framework positions adaptation as relational, context-dependent, and constrained by persistent social and structural conditions, thereby extending contemporary bereavement theory beyond individualistic psychological models.
